transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Alex Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Gupta (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (NorthStar CTO), Lena Ortiz (NorthStar ML Infra), Devon Brooks (NorthStar Product), Tariq Ahmed (NorthStar SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, imperfect): Discussed p95/p99 tail latency drivers; streaming vs non-streaming; KV cache warmup; batching knobs; quantization tradeoffs; network hops and VPC/private deployment implications. Agreed to run targeted p99 benchmarks and share security doc links.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to run a focused deep dive on tail latency — p95 and p99 — and walk through where Redwood's runtime makes a difference, and what you should watch for on the network/VPC side.
[00:12] Samir: Awesome thanks. We're seeing weird spikes in p99 on our prod calls, even though p50/p95 look fine, so, uh, hoping to root cause.
[00:20] Alex: Cool, can you sketch your current stack? That helps us map the hops.
[00:26] Lena: Sure, quick rundown: requests originate from our EU app load balancer, go through a gateway, then to our proxy fleet in VPC peering into your us-west region — we do cross-region for DR — then to Redwood hosted endpoints. Average RTT to Redwood is ~35ms but we sometimes see 80-120ms.
[00:42] Alex: Got it. A few immediate flags: cross-region plus extra proxies can add tail variance; also cold KV cache miss spikes can push p99 up.
[00:50] Devon: When you say KV cache miss, you mean Redwood's prefix cache?
[00:55] Priya: Yeah, KV cache for autoregressive models (we call it kv/kvcache) — if the cache isn't warmed or requests have long prompt prefixes, we see more KV reads that increase per-token latency. Also cache sharding and miss handling can create outliers.
[01:10] Samir: Hmm we do have long prompts, like 1.2k tokens average.
[01:15] Alex: That's a big piece — model sequence length distribution strongly impacts p99. Our runtime selects different kernels and memory paths for short vs long sequences; if you have wide variance some requests take slower code paths and those show up in tail stats.
[01:28] [01:28] Tariq: Are there recommended batch sizes? We're batching at the client side at 8 reqs, but latency goes up more than expected.
[01:36] Alex: Batching reduces amortized GPU overhead but increases head-of-line blocking when one request is long. For p99-focused SLAs we usually recommend smallish batching (2-4) with latency-aware routing; or dynamic batching with per-request latency SLOs.
[01:50] Samir: How about streaming vs non-streaming? We tried enabling streaming and saw slightly worse p99 last week.
[01:58] Priya: Streaming adds constant per-token flushes back over the network; it's great for p50/p95 perceived latency, but if you have noisy network hops (our earlier point) the per-token RTT multiplies and can blow up p99. Non-streaming returns the full response, so network overhead is one shot. So streaming helps perceived first-token times but can hurt tail if network is flaky.
[02:20] Lena: That matches our logs: first-token is generally okay but trailing tokens sometimes take ages.
[02:25] Maya: A typical pitfall is mixing large prefix sums with streaming over a multi-hop path. If you need deterministic p99, consider prefix caching + non-streaming or hybrid streaming (stream first chunk, then batch rest).
[02:38] Devon: You mentioned quantization earlier. Could that help p99?
[02:42] Priya: Yes and no. Lower-bit quantization reduces compute latency and throughput can increase, reducing contention and helping tail. But quantization changes kernel selection and memory layout; some quantized kernels may have slightly higher tail variance depending on hardware. We have profiles per model/hardware — for many weights int8 quantization on A10G gives 10-20% latency reduction p50 and reduces p99 in steady-state, but initial JIT/compilation steps can add spikes on cold starts.
[03:06] Samir: So for Private (on-prem) deployment, is cold JIT also a thing?
[03:10] Alex: Yes, the runtime's compilation and kernel selection are done on first-run per model/config. On private deployments you can precompile or pin kernels at deployment to avoid live JIT spikes. Redwood Dedicated supports pre-warming of kernels and KV cache priming.
[03:22] [03:22] Tariq: Network — earlier you mentioned network hops. What specifically should we measure and share?
[03:26] Maya: Traceroute and distribution of per-packet RTTs; number of NAT/GW hops; any layer 7 proxies doing buffering; egress behavior from your VPC and whether you're using VPC peering or PrivateLink. The fewer L4/L7 intermediaries, the more predictable tail.
[03:42] Lena: We're using a NAT GW then a proxy cluster then VPC peering. We'll get the traceroute.
[03:46] Alex: Great. Also collect per-request sizes — if you have many small/short requests interleaved with occasional huge ones, dynamic batching will sometimes combine them and cause head-of-line delays.
[03:59] Samir: Are there Redwood-specific metrics we should surface?
[04:02] Priya: Yes — we recommend shipping the Redwood X-Request-Id and sampling a few call traces with timing breakouts: ingress->routing->kv-lookup->compute->response. We can provide a trace hook to annotate per-stage timing.
[04:16] Devon: Is the KV cache async or blocking? We saw a few requests where CPU stalled while waiting for KV reads.
[04:22] Alex: The KV path is critical — it's usually a hot path in runtime. We try to serve KV from GPU memory where possible; otherwise a read from CPU/page cache is needed. For large prompt prefixes, KV lookups may trigger host-to-device transfers which add tens of ms. We have options: more aggressive KV co-location, eager prefetch for common prefixes, and hierarchical cache (local node + shared). For Dedicated deployments you can tune to ensure most active KV stays on-GPU.
[04:46] [04:46] Tariq: Any simple knobs we can change quickly?
[04:48] Maya: Short term: 1) reduce client-side max batch size to 2-4 for latency-sensitive routes, 2) enable prefix trimming or limit prompt length for critical flows, 3) try non-streaming for long responses, 4) enable quantized model variants on a test subset, 5) request a Redwood-located warmup traffic run to prime KV and kernels.
[05:08] Samir: Good. What about autoscaling and tail — does scale-up cause p99 blips?
[05:12] Priya: Spin-up of new GPU nodes can affect in-flight requests if routing changes mid-request. We recommend gradual scale policies and sticky routing during scale events; Dedicated also supports reserved pools to avoid cold nodes.
[05:25] Lena: For Private on-prem, we'd prefer predictable reserved capacity.
[05:28] Alex: That's what Dedicated/Private are for — reserved pods and preloaded kernels/KV.
[05:33] Maya: We also saw mention of SLO-weighted routing — you can route small-latency SLO requests to a low-latency pool and background high-throughput jobs to cheaper capacity.
[05:43] [05:43] Devon: Regarding measurement, do you have a recommended benchmark harness?
[05:47] Priya: We'll share a small harness (link: redwood.ai/bench-harness — note: placeholder) that runs p50/p95/p99, simulates client-side batching and network delays, and toggles streaming vs non-streaming. If you can run it from your VPC to our endpoint it will reproduce your network component.
[06:03] Samir: Perfect. Anything else on tail configs?
[06:06] Alex: For p99 specifically: 1) separate long-sequence and short-sequence traffic into different routes, 2) avoid mixing streaming with multi-hop networks, 3) pre-warm KV and kernels before peak, 4) use quantized models cautiously and benchmark output quality, 5) instrument per-stage timing.
[06:24] [06:24] Tariq: On security/VPC — if we go Private, how is traffic routed? Any extra hops?
[06:29] Maya: Private deployments can be VPC-peered or use PrivateLink; PrivateLink typically reduces network hops because it avoids NAT/Egress. On-prem options avoid cloud egress entirely but require you to host the runtime. We'll send the architecture diagram.
[06:42] Devon: We saw earlier that streaming had worse p99. Are there hybrid approaches?
[06:45] Priya: Hybrid streaming models work well — stream first N tokens to give perceived responsiveness, then return remainder in a single chunk, or stream at checkpoints. That reduces per-token round trips while preserving perceived interactivity.
[06:59] Samir: Ok makes sense. Can you detail what you'll run in your benchmark?
[07:02] Alex: We'll run 10k requests with your sequence length distribution, 50/50 short/long; measure p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU utilization, KV hit rate, and per-stage timings. We'll test: streaming vs non-streaming, quantized vs fp16, batch sizes 1/2/4, and with KV warm vs cold.
[07:20] Maya: We'll produce a spreadsheet with detailed percentiles and call out recommendations.
[07:24] Samir: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[07:27] Maya: Recap: Redwood runs benchmark (Alex), deliver by 2025-06-17; Maya sends pricing + security docs; NorthStar to share traceroute and egress details; follow-up meeting week of 2025-06-23 to review results.
[07:40] Devon: Thanks all.
[07:42] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with links and the harness.

End of transcript.
